q: What does a Hamiltonian cycle do?
options: Visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start
Visits every vertex at least once
explain: Using every edge exactly once is an Euler circuit, which is a different and much easier problem.

q: Which problem has a simple polynomial-time test?
options: Does the graph have an Euler circuit?
Does the graph have a Hamiltonian cycle?
Does the graph have a Hamiltonian path?
explain: A connected graph has an Euler circuit exactly when every vertex has even degree. The Hamiltonian problems are NP-complete.

q: How many Hamiltonian cycles does the complete graph K₅ have (each cycle counted once)?
explain: (n − 1)! / 2 = 4! / 2 = 12. 24 would count each cycle in both directions.

q: In the backtracking search, when is vertex u allowed as the next vertex on the path?
options: When u is adjacent to the last vertex and not already on the path
When u has the smallest degree
When u is adjacent to the start vertex
explain: Adjacency to the start is checked only at the very end, to close the cycle.

q: The path contains all n vertices. When is it a Hamiltonian cycle?
options: When its last vertex is adjacent to its first vertex
explain: Otherwise it is only a Hamiltonian path, and the search must backtrack.

q: Every connected graph in which every vertex has degree at least 2 has a Hamiltonian cycle.
explain: False. The Petersen graph is connected and 3-regular, yet has no Hamiltonian cycle.

q: Why does the complete bipartite graph K₂,₃ have no Hamiltonian cycle?
options: A cycle must alternate sides, so both sides need the same number of vertices
It has a vertex of degree 1
It has an odd number of edges
explain: Every edge goes between the two sides, so a cycle through all vertices would need 2 = 3.

q: What is the worst-case running time of the backtracking search on n vertices?
explain: It can try every ordering of the other n − 1 vertices. Dynamic programming over subsets improves this to O(2ⁿ · n²).

q: Each Hamiltonian cycle of an undirected graph is found twice by a search that does not check direction.
explain: True. From a fixed start, 1-2-3-4-1 and 1-4-3-2-1 are the same cycle. The page's code keeps only the version with path[1] < path[−1].

q: A knight's tour of a chessboard is an example of which problem?
explain: Squares are vertices and knight moves are edges. The tour must visit every square exactly once.
